title: Play, Fiddle, Play and the squeak D with the Binghamton Symphony
summary: In his cadenza Stewart climbs the top string past the violin's top note; Crouch recalls Hank Jones giving up at the top of the piano in a 1976 duo.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Now, you -- in terms of -- you performed "Play, Fiddle, Play" with the orchestra?

Yes. I performed that with the Binghamton Symphony and it was kind of a comical affair, you might say, because during my performance -- not the performance, but I might say, the rehearsal, this particular number that I was to perform with the Symphony was called "Play,

Fiddle, Play," and there is a spot in it towards the end where I have most of the goings-on by myself with the bass fiddle, which here's what really happens. I'm playing kind of a cadenza affair in which I will go up the string, the top string of my bass fiddle, and make notes as I go up to or I'm going to reach as high as I can to reach the highest note that I can on this top string, which I've worked on for many, many a year. As a matter of fact, I have reached notes on this top string of the bass fiddle which will sound or have sounded higher than what a little violin, the top note on the violin, can make. I go even higher with my bass fiddle.
What's the highest note you can play on your bass?
Well, the highest note, I call a squeak D.

And actually, it is -- that particular note is higher than a little violin can do normally. That is what I performed with the Binghamton Symphony and even during rehearsal, I meant to say that when I was reaching for this note, towards the end, I would ask one of the violins to copy me and do you know that when I made this squeak D, the violinist was unable to make that note -- duplicate that note on his little violin?
Yeah, I remember when you were during that when I heard you in 1976 with Hank Jones in a duo.
And you would play and he would play at the piano.
And then finally he got in the piano --
He got to the top of the piano and he couldn't play anymore.
He threw his hands up and he says, 'Well, I can't go any further.'
At that point, you played one more note up there.
Yeah, I played another octave or two, yeah.
